2º de Bachillerato · Inglés II · Tema 2

Modal verbs and modal perfects

Nombre: ______________________   Fecha: ___________

Qué vas a aprender

  • Reconocer las características gramaticales de los verbos modales y de sus equivalentes (have to, need to, be able to)
  • Expresar capacidad, permiso, obligación, prohibición, necesidad y consejo con el matiz adecuado
  • Hacer deducciones sobre el presente y el pasado con must, can't, may, might y could
  • Usar los modal perfects para criticar, lamentar y hablar de oportunidades perdidas
  • Formar modales en voz pasiva y en forma continua
  • Resolver reescrituras tipo PAU y matizar opiniones en un writing con verbos modales

Para pensar

«You needn't have bought bread» y «You didn't need to buy bread» parecen iguales. ¿Cuál dice que el pan ya está en casa?

Explicación

2.1 Qué son los verbos modales

Los verbos modales (can, could, may, might, must, shall, should, will, would, y también ought to y need en algunos usos) no expresan acciones, sino la actitud del hablante: si algo es posible, obligatorio, probable, permitido o aconsejable.

Tienen rasgos gramaticales propios: no llevan -s en tercera persona (She can swim); van seguidos del infinitivo sin to (You must go), salvo ought to; forman la negativa y la interrogativa sin do (Can I…? You shouldn't…); y no tienen infinitivo, participio ni todos los tiempos. Por eso no se puede decir *I will can ni *I have must.

Cuando necesitamos un tiempo que el modal no tiene, usamos un equivalente (semi-modal): be able to (capacidad), have to (obligación), need to (necesidad), be allowed to (permiso). I will be able to help you tomorrow. She has had to work late all week. You won't be allowed to use your phone.

Un mismo modal puede tener dos tipos de significado: uno sobre obligación, permiso o capacidad (You must wear a helmet) y otro sobre probabilidad o deducción (You must be tired). Este tema recorre los dos.

2.2 Capacidad: can, could, be able to y manage to

Can expresa capacidad en el presente (She can speak four languages) y could, capacidad general en el pasado (I could read when I was four). Para los demás tiempos se usa be able to: I haven't been able to sleep. One day robots will be able to think.

Matiz importante para la PAU: cuando hablamos de un logro concreto en una ocasión del pasado (conseguir hacer algo con esfuerzo), no se usa could en afirmativa, sino was able to o managed to: The fire spread quickly, but everyone was able to escape / managed to escape. En negativa sí vale couldn't: I couldn't open the door.

Con verbos de percepción (see, hear, smell, feel) y de entendimiento (understand, remember) se usa can / could en lugar del continuo: I can hear music next door. I could smell smoke.

Para hablar de una capacidad que no se usó en el pasado se emplea could have + participio: You could have won the race if you hadn't slowed down. Lo veremos con más detalle en el apartado de los modal perfects.

2.3 Permiso y peticiones

Para pedir permiso, de lo más informal a lo más formal: Can I open the window? Could I open the window? May I open the window? Might I…? (muy formal y poco frecuente). Para darlo o negarlo: You can / may go. You can't / may not use a dictionary.

Cuando hablamos de normas o de permiso en otros tiempos, usamos be allowed to o be permitted to: We weren't allowed to leave the room during the exam. Students are not permitted to bring phones. Para el pasado general, could: When I was a child, I could stay up late at weekends. Pero para una ocasión concreta, was allowed to: Yesterday I was allowed to stay up late.

Las peticiones corteses usan formas «más distantes»: Can you help me? → Could you help me? → Would you mind helping me? → I was wondering if you could help me. Fíjate en que Would you mind va seguido de -ing y que la respuesta afirmativa es No, not at all (no me importa).

Para ofrecer y sugerir se usa shall en preguntas con I / we: Shall I carry your bag? Shall we go?, sobre todo en inglés británico.

2.4 Obligación y prohibición: must, have to, mustn't y don't have to

Must expresa una obligación que impone el propio hablante o una norma escrita: I must study harder (lo pienso yo). Passengers must fasten their seat belts (normas oficiales). Have to expresa una obligación externa: I have to wear a uniform at school (la impone el centro). En muchos contextos son intercambiables, pero must solo existe en presente: en pasado y futuro se usa had to y will have to.

En negativa, el significado se separa por completo. Mustn't es una prohibición: You mustn't smoke here. Don't have to indica ausencia de obligación: You don't have to come if you don't want to (no es necesario).

FormaSignificadoEjemplo
mustobligación (hablante, normas)I must call my grandmother.
have to / have got toobligación externaWe have to hand it in by Friday.
mustn'tprohibiciónYou mustn't park here.
don't have tono es obligatorioYou don't have to pay; it's free.
be supposed tolo que se espera según una normaYou're supposed to be in class now.

Be supposed to expresa lo que debería ocurrir según una regla o un acuerdo, a menudo con la idea de que no se cumple: We were supposed to meet at six, but she didn't turn up.

2.5 Necesidad: need, needn't y needn't have

Need puede funcionar como verbo normal (need to) o como modal (sobre todo en negativa, needn't). You need to renew your passport. You don't need to / needn't bring anything. Needn't es más frecuente en inglés británico y en registro formal.

En pasado aparece el contraste que vimos en la pregunta inicial. Didn't need to + base indica que algo no era necesario; generalmente no se hizo: I didn't need to take a taxi, so I walked. Needn't have + participio indica que algo se hizo aunque no hacía falta: I needn't have taken a taxi: the station was just round the corner (lo cogí, y fue inútil).

Need + -ing con sentido pasivo es otro uso avanzado: The car needs washing (= needs to be washed). Your hair needs cutting.

En el writing formal, en lugar de repetir must, conviene variar con expresiones de necesidad: It is essential / vital / crucial that…, There is an urgent need for…, It is necessary to… Por ejemplo: It is essential that governments invest in public transport.

2.6 Consejo y recomendación: should, ought to y had better

Should y ought to dan consejos, recomendaciones u opiniones sobre lo correcto: You should see a doctor. We ought to protect endangered species. Son casi equivalentes; ought to es algo más formal y menos frecuente en preguntas y negativas.

Had better ('d better) + base es más fuerte: un consejo urgente para una situación concreta, con la idea de que habrá consecuencias si no se sigue. You'd better hurry or you'll miss the bus. La negativa es had better not: You'd better not tell anyone. Aunque lleva had, se refiere al presente o al futuro.

Should también expresa probabilidad o expectativa: The parcel should arrive tomorrow (es lo previsto). She's been studying all year, so she should pass.

En los ensayos de opinión, should es el modal clave para proponer soluciones: Schools should teach financial education. Governments ought to ban single-use plastics. Para sonar más formal, alterna con It is advisable to…, It would be a good idea to…, I would recommend + -ing.

2.7 Deducción sobre el presente

Los modales permiten expresar lo seguros que estamos de algo a partir de unas pistas. Es uno de los usos más típicos del nivel B2 y aparece mucho en las reescrituras.

Must: estamos casi seguros de que algo es verdad. The lights are on, so they must be at home. Can't: estamos casi seguros de que no lo es. He can't be hungry; he's just had lunch. Atención: lo contrario de must en deducción es can't, no *mustn't.

May, might y could: es posible, pero no estamos seguros. She may / might / could be in the library. Might suele indicar algo menos probable que may. En negativa, may not y might not expresan posibilidad negativa: She might not know about the meeting. (Couldn't sería imposibilidad.)

Para deducir sobre una acción en curso, se usa la forma continua: He's not answering. He must be driving. They can't be sleeping; it's noon.

Reescrituras habituales: I'm sure she's tired → She must be tired. It's impossible that he's the thief → He can't be the thief. Perhaps they are lost → They may / might be lost.

2.8 Deducción sobre el pasado: must have, can't have, might have

Para deducir sobre el pasado, el modal va seguido de have + participio (modal perfect): la estructura no cambia según la persona.

Must have done: seguro que pasó. The streets are wet. It must have rained during the night. Can't / couldn't have done: imposible que pasara. She can't have seen me; she was looking the other way. May / might / could have done: quizá pasó. I can't find my keys. I might have left them at school.

Con la forma continua: must have been + -ing. Your eyes are red. You must have been crying. He can't have been listening.

Cuidado con could have done: puede ser una deducción (The thief could have entered through the window, es posible) o una capacidad no utilizada (You could have called me!, podías haberlo hecho y no lo hiciste). El contexto lo aclara.

Reescrituras tipo PAU: I'm sure he forgot → He must have forgotten. It's impossible that they finished so soon → They can't have finished so soon. Perhaps she missed the bus → She may / might have missed the bus.

2.9 Crítica, arrepentimiento y oportunidades perdidas

Should have / ought to have + participio expresa que algo era lo correcto y no se hizo; sirve para criticar o lamentarse. You should have told me the truth. I ought to have studied more. En negativa, se hizo algo que no era correcto: I shouldn't have eaten so much.

Could have + participio habla de una posibilidad que no se aprovechó: We could have gone to the beach, but we stayed at home. Con tono de reproche: You could have helped me!

Would have + participio expresa lo que habría ocurrido en otras circunstancias (tercer condicional, tema 3): I would have come, but nobody invited me. Wouldn't have se usa para algo que no habría pasado: I wouldn't have known without your help.

Modal perfectIdeaEjemplo
should have donecrítica / arrepentimientoI should have revised.
shouldn't have donese hizo algo incorrectoYou shouldn't have shouted.
could have doneoportunidad perdidaWe could have won.
would have doneresultado hipotéticoI'd have helped you.
needn't have doneesfuerzo innecesarioYou needn't have waited.

2.10 Otros usos de will, would, may y might

Will y would expresan comportamientos característicos o hábitos, a veces con un matiz de irritación: She'll spend hours talking on the phone. When I was little, my grandmother would tell us stories every night. Con acento enfático, crítica: He WILL leave his socks on the floor!

Won't / wouldn't expresan negativa a hacer algo, incluso con objetos: The car won't start. My little brother wouldn't eat his vegetables.

May / might as well significa que algo es lo más razonable porque no hay una opción mejor: The last bus has gone, so we might as well walk. May… but sirve para hacer una concesión en un argumento: Technology may be useful, but it also isolates us.

Otras expresiones semimodales de probabilidad: be bound to (seguro que…: It's bound to rain at the weekend), be likely / unlikely to (Prices are likely to rise), there's a good chance that…. Son muy útiles en los writings para expresar predicciones con matices.

2.11 Modales en pasiva y en forma continua

Los modales se combinan con la voz pasiva (tema 4) con la estructura modal + be + participio: The rules must be respected. This problem can't be solved easily. Phones should be switched off. En pasado: modal + have been + participio: The letter must have been sent by mistake. The accident could have been avoided.

Con la forma continua, modal + be + -ing en presente y modal + have been + -ing en pasado: They should be arriving soon. He must have been working all night.

PresentePasado
Activa simplemust domust have done
Activa continuamust be doingmust have been doing
Pasivamust be donemust have been done

Estas formas aparecen a menudo en textos de la PAU de tipo periodístico o científico, porque permiten dar opiniones impersonales: More should be done to protect the oceans. The ancient city may have been destroyed by an earthquake. Reconocerlas ayuda a responder bien las preguntas de comprensión.

2.12 Los modales en la PAU: reescribir y matizar

En las tareas de reescritura (rephrasing) los modales sustituyen expresiones de certeza, posibilidad, obligación o consejo. Las transformaciones más frecuentes son:

Frase originalCon modal
I'm sure he was at home.He must have been at home.
It's impossible that she said that.She can't have said that.
Perhaps they have left.They may / might have left.
It wasn't a good idea to shout.You shouldn't have shouted.
It wasn't necessary to cook, but I did.I needn't have cooked.
It isn't compulsory to wear a tie.You don't have to wear a tie.
If I were you, I'd apologise.You should / ought to apologise.

En el writing, los modales sirven para matizar (hedging): un buen ensayo evita afirmaciones absolutas. Compara Video games make children violent con Some video games may contribute to aggressive behaviour. La segunda es más prudente y académica.

Consejo práctico: antes de escribir el modal, decide primero la función (deducción, obligación, consejo, crítica) y el tiempo (presente o pasado). Después elige la forma: modal + base para el presente y modal + have + participio para el pasado.

Los verbos modales de un vistazo

Ejercicios

  1. Completa: «___ I use your pen?» (pedir permiso con cortesía)

  2. Completa: «You ___ smoke in hospitals. It's forbidden.»

  3. Completa: «Tomorrow is Sunday, so I ___ get up early.»

  4. Completa: «When I was six, I ___ ride a bike.»

  5. Completa: «You look ill. You ___ see a doctor.»

  6. Completa: «She has a Ferrari. She ___ be rich.»

  7. Completa: «He ___ be at work; I've just seen him at the gym.»

  8. Completa: «Take an umbrella. It ___ rain later.»

  9. Completa con be able to: «I'm sorry, I ___ come to your party next Saturday.»

  10. Corrige: «She cans speak Chinese.»

  11. Completa: «We ___ (have to) wear a uniform at my old school.»

  12. Completa: «You'd ___ hurry or you'll be late.»

  13. Reescribe: «I'm sure they were tired after the trip.»

  14. Reescribe: «It's impossible that he wrote this essay alone.»

  15. Reescribe: «Perhaps she didn't hear the phone.»

  16. Reescribe: «It was a mistake not to book in advance.» → «We ___.»

  17. Explica la diferencia: «I didn't need to wait» / «I needn't have waited».

  18. Completa: «The car ___ (not / start) this morning, so I took the bus.»

  19. Completa: «We were ___ to meet at six, but she didn't come.»

  20. Reescribe: «It isn't necessary to print the tickets.» con needn't.

  21. Completa: «Despite the storm, the pilot ___ land the plane safely.»

  22. Completa: «He's not answering. He ___ (drive).»

  23. Completa: «Your hair needs ___ (cut).»

  24. Reescribe: «Would you mind ___ (close) the window?»

  25. Reescribe en pasiva: «They must have built this castle in the 12th century.»

  26. Reescribe: «I regret not accepting that job.» con should.

  27. Completa con el modal perfect adecuado: «You ___ (tell) me it was a formal party! I'm wearing jeans!»

  28. Explica la diferencia: «She could have taken the train» como deducción y como oportunidad perdida.

  29. Reescribe matizando para un ensayo: «Social media causes depression in teenagers.»

  30. Completa: «The museum is closed and it's raining, so we ___ go home.»

  31. Corrige los cuatro errores: «You mustn't to pay; it's free. He must forgotten his keys. I could finish the marathon last year. She can't been there.»

  32. Escribe un párrafo de 60 palabras sobre un error que cometiste, usando should have, could have y needn't have.

Explícalo con tus palabras

Incluye: Qué rasgos gramaticales comparten todos los verbos modales; Por qué mustn't y don't have to significan cosas distintas; Cómo se expresa la deducción en presente y en pasado; Qué diferencia hay entre should have, could have y needn't have; Cómo se forma un modal en voz pasiva.

Resumen

Glosario

Modal verb
Verbo auxiliar que expresa actitud: posibilidad, obligación, permiso…
Semi-modal
Equivalente con tiempos completos: have to, be able to, need to.
Ability
Capacidad: can, could, be able to.
Permission
Permiso: can, could, may, be allowed to.
Obligation
Obligación: must, have to.
Prohibition
Prohibición: mustn't, can't, not be allowed to.
Lack of necessity
Ausencia de necesidad: don't have to, needn't.
Advice
Consejo: should, ought to, had better.
Deduction
Conclusión a partir de pistas: must, can't, might.
Modal perfect
Modal + have + participio para hablar del pasado.
Criticism
Crítica sobre el pasado: should have, could have.
Missed opportunity
Oportunidad perdida: could have done.
Be supposed to
Lo que se espera según una norma o acuerdo.
Be bound to
Ser casi seguro que ocurra.
Hedging
Matizar las afirmaciones en un texto académico.

Tarjetas de repaso

Recórtalas: pregunta delante, respuesta detrás.

can / could / be able toCapacidad; logro concreto: was able to.
must vs have toObligación interna o normas / externa.
mustn'tProhibición.
don't have to / needn'tNo es necesario.
needn't have doneSe hizo y no hacía falta.
should / ought toConsejo u opinión.
had betterConsejo urgente: You'd better go.
must (deducción)Casi seguro: She must be tired.
can't (deducción)Imposible: He can't be serious.
must have doneDeducción sobre el pasado.
should have doneCrítica o arrepentimiento.
modal + be donePasiva: It must be done today.

Soluciones

  1. C) Modal sin -s ni to.
  2. A) Futuro: be able to.
  3. D) Logro concreto.
  4. B) Permiso cortés.
  5. B) Would you mind + -ing.
  6. D) Prohibición.
  7. A) Sin obligación.
  8. C) Hecho innecesario.
  9. D) Had better not + base.
  10. B) Should: expectativa.
  11. C) Deducción negativa.
  12. A) Deducción positiva.
  13. C) Posibilidad.
  14. A) Deducción pasada.
  15. D) Imposibilidad pasada.
  16. B) Crítica.
  17. B) Oportunidad perdida.
  18. D) Modal pasivo.
  19. A) Modal perfect pasivo.
  20. C) La opción más razonable.

Soluciones de los ejercicios

  1. Could (o May): petición de permiso cortés.
  2. mustn't: prohibición.
  3. don't have to: no es obligatorio.
  4. could: capacidad general en el pasado.
  5. should (o ought to): consejo.
  6. must: deducción con certeza.
  7. can't: deducción negativa.
  8. may / might: posibilidad.
  9. won't be able to: futuro de can.
  10. She can speak Chinese: los modales no llevan -s.
  11. had to: pasado de must / have to.
  12. better: had better, consejo urgente.
  13. They must have been tired after the trip.
  14. He can't (couldn't) have written this essay alone.
  15. She may not / might not have heard the phone.
  16. We should have booked in advance.
  17. La primera: no hacía falta esperar (probablemente no esperé). La segunda: esperé, pero no hacía falta.
  18. wouldn't start: negativa (de un objeto) en el pasado.
  19. supposed: be supposed to, lo acordado que no se cumplió.
  20. You needn't print the tickets.
  21. was able to / managed to: logro concreto.
  22. must be driving: deducción sobre una acción en curso.
  23. cutting: need + -ing con sentido pasivo.
  24. closing: Would you mind + -ing.
  25. This castle must have been built in the 12th century.
  26. I should have accepted that job.
  27. could have told / should have told: reproche.
  28. Deducción: es posible que cogiera el tren. Oportunidad perdida: podía cogerlo, pero no lo hizo. El contexto decide.
  29. Modelo: Excessive use of social media may contribute to depression in some teenagers.
  30. might as well: es la opción más razonable.
  31. You don't have to pay; He must have forgotten his keys; I managed to / was able to finish the marathon; She can't have been there.
  32. Modelo: Last year I left my History project until the last minute. I should have started earlier, and I could have asked my teacher for help. I stayed up all night, but I needn't have panicked: the deadline had been extended. Next time I'll organise my time better.
